messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret Dwyer had spent most of her adult life working as a public defender, a career that had trained her to keep her composure in tense rooms and to read danger quickly. At seventy-eight, she still moved through her days with the brisk, disciplined air of someone used to deadlines and crowded hallways, but since the assault she had begun to feel the city itself as charged and watchful. The attack had happened on an ordinary evening, after she had left her office late and was walking to her car with her briefcase tucked under one arm. A man came up behind her in a stretch of parking lot where the lights were weak and the other cars stood dark and close together. He grabbed her hard enough to wrench her shoulder and shoved her against the side of the vehicle, close enough that she could smell his sweat and the stale smoke on his jacket. The memory that stayed with her was not only the force of it, but the sudden certainty that she could not see who was behind her or what he might do next.

In the months afterward, Margaret found herself looking over her shoulder almost without thinking, especially when she was alone in public places or crossing a lot after work. She would glance behind her in the hallway outside the courthouse, in the supermarket aisle, even on the short walk from the office elevator to the street, as though some part of her expected the same unseen hand to come from behind. What made it worse was the way she began watching other people closely for any sign they might mean her harm: a man lingering near a doorway, someone walking too close on the sidewalk, a stranger who looked at her for a second too long. At work, where she once could focus on a client’s case without distraction, she now found herself measuring faces and posture before she could settle into the legal problem in front of her. The vigilance took up so much of her attention that it colored her whole day, leaving her exhausted by afternoon and uneasy in ways she could not easily shake.

Margaret was ashamed by how jumpy she had become. A sudden footstep in the office corridor, a car backfiring outside her building, a hand dropped unexpectedly on her arm from behind would make her flinch sharply, her heart kicking hard before she could catch herself. She described herself as “on a wire,” always braced, as if she had to be ready for the next blow even while sitting at her desk with case files spread out in front of her. The reaction felt absurd to her, especially because she had spent decades advising clients who lived with real danger and had always prided herself on being steady. Yet the steadiness now seemed to have gone missing, replaced by an unsettled alertness that made sleep harder and ordinary errands feel like small ordeals.

Over time, the habits she developed to manage that fear began to narrow her life. She chose parking spaces near entrances, avoided walking alone after dusk, and lingered inside her office until the building emptied enough that she felt less exposed. In the courthouse, she took longer routes that let her see who was approaching, and at the grocery store she kept her cart between herself and other shoppers when she could. Her husband noticed that she no longer volunteered to meet friends for evening dinners and that she became tense on the rare occasions when they were delayed and had to cross a dark lot. Margaret could not fully explain the change except to say that after what happened, she no longer trusted the moments when she could not monitor the space around her. She remained frightened, too, by the possibility that her body would betray her again in front of colleagues or strangers, the sudden startle making her feel foolish and exposed.

By the time she sought help, Margaret had come to the conclusion that she was living as if the assault might recur at any moment, and that this way of moving through the world was steadily shrinking what remained of her independence. What brought her in was not only the discomfort, but the growing fear that her constant scanning was becoming the new normal. She hoped to feel safe enough to walk to her car without checking behind her at every few steps, and she feared that if nothing changed, she would keep becoming more vigilant, more jumpy, and more confined to the narrow routes that already felt tolerable.
